blocks.text: The air swirling into a vacuum-cleaner nozzle, the water draining out of a bathtub and the flow around the end of a wing tip can all be sketched, to a first approximation, by adding together a handful of simple flow patterns whose formulas fit on one line. Each pattern is a solution of one linear equation, so the engineer can build realistic flows with arithmetic. This unit introduces the building blocks and the test for whether a flow can be treated this way.

blocks.markdown: Many flows of low-viscosity fluids away from walls are well described by **ideal** (inviscid) flow. If the flow is also **irrotational**, meaning fluid elements do not rotate as they move, the velocity can be obtained from a scalar function, the **velocity potential** $\phi$. Together with the stream function $\psi$ (for two-dimensional incompressible flow) this gives two scalar functions from which the velocity follows by differentiation.

blocks.title: Vorticity and irrotational flow
blocks.text: In two dimensions the vorticity (twice the local rotation rate of a fluid element) is $\zeta=\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}$ (1/s). A flow is **irrotational** if $\zeta=0$ everywhere. Then there exists a potential $\phi$ with $\mathbf V=\nabla\phi$, i.e. $u=\partial\phi/\partial x$, $v=\partial\phi/\partial y$ in Cartesian coordinates and $v_r=\partial\phi/\partial r$, $v_\theta=\frac1r\partial\phi/\partial\theta$ in polar coordinates.

blocks.latex: u=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y},\qquad v=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x},\qquad \nabla^2\phi=0,\quad\nabla^2\psi=0
blocks.caption: Potential and stream function: Cauchy-Riemann relations; both satisfy Laplace's equation for 2D incompressible irrotational flow

blocks.markdown:
Continuity for incompressible flow, $
abla\cdot\mathbf V=0$, substituted into $\mathbf V=
abla\phi$ gives $
abla^2\phi=0$ (Laplace's equation). Irrotationality substituted into $u=\psi_y$, $v=-\psi_x$ gives $
abla^2\psi=0$. Lines of constant $\phi$ (**equipotentials**) and of constant $\psi$ (streamlines) cross at right angles. Because Laplace's equation is linear, solutions can be superposed.

blocks.title: Velocity components from a potential
blocks.prompt: An ideal two-dimensional flow has the velocity potential phi = 4x + x^2 - y^2 (SI units). Find u and v, verify that the flow is incompressible, find the stream function with psi = 0 at the origin, and find the velocity at (x, y) = (1, 2) m.

steps.text: Differentiate the potential to get the velocity components.
Check continuity: du/dx + dv/dy = 2 + (-2) = 0, so the flow is incompressible; this also reflects Laplace's equation for phi.
Integrate u = dpsi/dy with respect to y, then fix the function of x using v = -dpsi/dx: -2y - g'(x) = -2y so g' = 0.
At (1, 2): the components and speed follow from the formulas above.

blocks.markdown: **Elementary flows.** Three simple solutions are the building blocks. (i) A **uniform stream** of speed $U$ along $x$: $\phi=Ux$, $\psi=Uy$. (ii) A **source** (or **sink** if $m<0$) of strength $m$ (m$^2$/s, the volume flow per unit depth), at the origin: the fluid moves radially outward with $v_r=m/(2\pi r)$ since the flow $2\pi r\,v_r$ across any circle equals $m$. (iii) A **free (irrotational) vortex** of circulation $\Gamma$ (m$^2$/s): the fluid circles the origin with $v_\theta=\Gamma/(2\pi r)$, so that $2\pi r\,v_\theta=\Gamma$ is the same on every circle. Both the source and the vortex are singular at $r=0$.

blocks.caption: Elementary plane potential flows (polar coordinates; strengths m and Gamma in m^2/s)

blocks.title: A source and the pressure field around it
blocks.prompt: A line source of strength 0.80 m^2/s discharges water (density 998 kg/m^3) into an unbounded ideal flow. Find the radial speed at r = 0.25 m and r = 1.00 m, and the pressure difference between those radii using Bernoulli's equation.

steps.text: Radial speed from the source formula at the two radii.
Bernoulli's equation along a streamline (horizontal flow, no body force): p + rho V^2/2 is constant, so the pressure rises with radius as the speed falls.

blocks.answer: v(0.25 m) = 0.5093 m/s, v(1.00 m) = 0.1273 m/s, and the pressure at r = 1.00 m is 121.3 Pa higher.

blocks.markdown: **Testing for irrotationality.** Given a velocity field, compute $\zeta=\partial v/\partial x-\partial u/\partial y$. For example, $u=x^2-y^2$, $v=-2xy$ gives $\zeta=-2y-(-2y)=0$, so the flow is irrotational (and also incompressible, since $2x-2x=0$); it has the potential $\phi=x^3/3-xy^2$. The simple shear $u=3y$, $v=0$ has $\zeta=-3$ s$^{-1}$, so it is rotational: elements spin as they are sheared, and no potential exists. For the free vortex, $v_\theta=\Gamma/(2\pi r)$, the vorticity (in polar form $\zeta=\frac1r\frac{d(rv_\theta)}{dr}$) is zero for every $r>0$ because $rv_\theta$ is constant. The fluid circulates but does not rotate; the origin is the only singular point.

items: Test for continuity: $\partial u/\partial x+\partial v/\partial y=0$.
Test for irrotationality: $\partial v/\partial x-\partial u/\partial y=0$.
If both hold, find $\phi$ or $\psi$ by integration and check Laplace's equation.
Add elementary flows to build complex ones, since the equations are linear.

blocks.title: Pressure from Bernoulli everywhere
blocks.text: In irrotational flow Bernoulli's equation $p+\tfrac12\rho V^2+\rho gz=\text{const}$ holds between any two points in the flow, not only along a single streamline. So once the velocity field is known from $\phi$, the pressure field follows immediately.

blocks.title: Mind the singularities
blocks.text: The source and the free vortex have infinite velocity at $r=0$. Real fluid never behaves this way: near the centre of a real vortex viscosity forces solid-body rotation (a vortex core), and real sources have a finite size. Use the formulas only outside such regions.

points: For irrotational flow, $\mathbf V=\nabla\phi$, giving $u=\partial\phi/\partial x$, $v=\partial\phi/\partial y$; with $\psi$, $u=\psi_y$, $v=-\psi_x$.
Incompressible irrotational flows satisfy Laplace's equation, $\nabla^2\phi=\nabla^2\psi=0$, so elementary solutions can be added.
Source: $v_r=m/(2\pi r)$; free vortex: $v_\theta=\Gamma/(2\pi r)$; uniform stream: $\phi=Ux$, $\psi=Uy$.
A flow is irrotational if $\zeta=\partial v/\partial x-\partial u/\partial y=0$; the free vortex is irrotational everywhere except the centre.

questions.stem: For an irrotational two-dimensional flow with velocity potential phi(x, y), how are the Cartesian velocity components obtained?

distractorRationale.a: This does not produce a vector field; the components are the separate partial derivatives.
distractorRationale.b: This is how u and v follow from the stream function, with u = dpsi/dy and v = -dpsi/dx.
distractorRationale.c: The potential is defined with a positive gradient, V = grad phi, so no minus sign appears.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the velocity is the gradient of the potential.

questions.explanation: The velocity potential is defined by $\mathbf V=\nabla\phi$, so $u=\partial\phi/\partial x$ and $v=\partial\phi/\partial y$. The stream function, by contrast, uses $u=\partial\psi/\partial y$, $v=-\partial\psi/\partial x$.

questions.stem: An ideal plane flow has the velocity potential phi = 0.5 x^3 - 1.5 x y^2 (SI units). Find the speed in m/s at the point (x, y) = (2.0 m, 1.0 m).
A line source of strength 2.5 m^2/s (volume flow per unit depth) is located at the origin of an ideal incompressible flow. Find the radial velocity at a distance r = 0.40 m in m/s.
questions.explanation: Continuity requires 2 pi r v_r = m, so v_r = m/(2 pi r) = 2.5/(2 pi x 0.40) = 0.9947 m/s.

questions.stem: A free vortex of circulation 6.0 m^2/s turns water in a horizontal plane. Find the tangential velocity at r = 1.5 m from the centre in m/s.
questions.explanation: For a free vortex v_theta = Gamma/(2 pi r) = 6.0/(2 pi x 1.5) = 0.6366 m/s. The speed falls inversely with distance.

questions.stem: What does a negative strength m mean for a source-type potential flow v_r = m/(2 pi r)?

options.text: The fluid flows radially inward: it is a sink

questions.correctOptionText: The fluid flows radially inward: it is a sink

distractorRationale.a: A sink is still incompressible; mass is removed at the singular point only.
distractorRationale.b: Circulation about a point is described by the vortex strength, not by the source strength.
distractorRationale.c: The sign of m does not alter irrotationality; both are irrotational.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: a sink is a source with negative strength.

questions.explanation: With $m<0$ the radial velocity is negative, meaning fluid flows towards the origin, i.e. a sink. The flow remains irrotational and incompressible away from the origin.

questions.stem: Which of the following two-dimensional velocity fields is irrotational? (x and y in metres, velocities in m/s.)

distractorRationale.a: dv/dx = 1 and du/dy = 2y, which is zero only on the line y = 0.5.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: dv/dx = 3 and du/dy = 3, so the vorticity is zero.
distractorRationale.c: dv/dx = -3 and du/dy = 3 gives a vorticity of -6 per second.
distractorRationale.d: This simple shear has vorticity -3 per second.

questions.explanation: The test is $\zeta=\partial v/\partial x-\partial u/\partial y=0$. Only the first field gives $3-3=0$; the others give $-6$, $-3$ and $1-2y$, respectively.

questions.stem: A free vortex flow v_theta = Gamma/(2 pi r) is irrotational at every point except the centre, even though the fluid circulates around it.
questions.explanation: For this field $rv_\theta=\Gamma/2\pi$ is constant, so the polar-coordinate vorticity $\frac1r\frac{d(rv_\theta)}{dr}$ vanishes for $r>0$. The fluid elements travel in circles but do not spin about their own centres.

questions.stem: How does the speed in a free vortex vary with the distance r from its centre?

options.text: It is inversely proportional to r
It is inversely proportional to r squared
It is directly proportional to r

questions.correctOptionText: It is inversely proportional to r

distractorRationale.b: That is the dependence of the source or doublet strength terms, not the free vortex.
distractorRationale.c: A free vortex has a speed that varies with radius.
distractorRationale.d: This is solid-body rotation (a rotational flow), not a free vortex.

questions.explanation: The circulation $2\pi rv_\theta=\Gamma$ is the same around every circle, so $v_\theta=\Gamma/(2\pi r)$: it falls as $1/r$ and rises without bound as $r\to0$, where a real vortex has a viscous core.

questions.stem: For a two-dimensional, incompressible, irrotational flow show that the velocity potential and the stream function both satisfy Laplace's equation, and that equipotential lines are perpendicular to streamlines.
markingGuide: Irrotational: dv/dx - du/dy = 0, so a potential exists with u = dphi/dx, v = dphi/dy
Continuity du/dx + dv/dy = 0 with u, v from phi gives d2phi/dx2 + d2phi/dy2 = 0
Stream function u = dpsi/dy, v = -dpsi/dx satisfies continuity automatically
Irrotationality with psi gives -d2psi/dx2 - d2psi/dy2 = 0, i.e. Laplace's equation
Cauchy-Riemann relations dphi/dx = dpsi/dy and dphi/dy = -dpsi/dx
Gradients of phi and psi are perpendicular: (u, v) . (-v, u) = 0, so lines of constant phi and psi intersect at right angles
questions.explanation:
Substituting $u=\phi_x$, $v=\phi_y$ into continuity gives $
abla^2\phi=0$, and substituting $u=\psi_y$, $v=-\psi_x$ into the zero-vorticity condition gives $
abla^2\psi=0$. Because $
abla\phi\cdot
abla\psi=\phi_x\psi_x+\phi_y\psi_y=-uv+vu=0$, the lines of constant $\phi$ and $\psi$ are orthogonal.

questions.stem: A spiral flow is formed by superposing a source of strength 1.2 m^2/s and a counter-clockwise free vortex of circulation 4.0 m^2/s, both at the origin. (a) Write the velocity components. (b) Calculate the radial and tangential velocities and the speed at r = 0.80 m, and the angle of the velocity to the radial direction. (c) Show that this flow is irrotational for r > 0.
markingGuide: Superposition: v_r = m/(2 pi r), v_theta = Gamma/(2 pi r)
At r = 0.80 m: v_r = 0.2387 m/s and v_theta = 0.7958 m/s
Angle to the radial direction = atan(v_theta/v_r) = 73.3 degrees (constant for all r)
Vorticity = (1/r) d(r v_theta)/dr = 0 since r v_theta = Gamma/(2 pi) is constant (and v_r gives no vorticity)
Therefore irrotational for r > 0, so the flow derives from phi = (m/2pi) ln r + (Gamma/2pi) theta
questions.explanation: At r = 0.80 m the radial speed is 0.2387 m/s and the tangential speed 0.7958 m/s, giving a speed of 0.8308 m/s at 73.3 degrees to the radius. The product r v_theta is constant, so the polar vorticity vanishes and the superposed flow is irrotational away from the origin.
